slides.eyebrow: No one talks about this, but:
slides.sub: Use it on a $500K home and your estimate is off by more than $25,000. Here's the rate to use.
slides.source: NJ Division of Taxation, 2025 tax rates

slides.title: 1. The general rate
slides.body: This is the tax per [[$100 of assessed value]]. Your bill is this rate times the assessed value, divided by 100. Where assessments trail today's prices, it looks huge. Cranford's 2025 general rate: 7.248.
slides.source: NJ Division of Taxation, Property Tax Statistics

slides.title: 2. The effective rate
slides.body: This one shows the rate as if every town were assessed at full market value. It's the rate to [[compare towns]] with, not to figure a bill. Cranford's 2025 effective rate: 2.106.
slides.source: NJ Division of Taxation, 2025 tax rates

slides.title: 3. Do the rough math
slides.body: A $500,000 home x 2.106% = [[about $10,530 a year]]. Putting the general rate on the price gives you $36,240, which is way off.
slides.source: Math from NJ Division of Taxation 2025 rates

slides.title: 4. Check the real bill
slides.body: Rates get you close. Before you offer, ask for the [[home's actual tax bill]] and its assessment. Talk to a licensed lender for your numbers.

caption:
No one talks about this, but every NJ town has 2 property tax rates. Cranford's 2025 general rate is 7.248. Its effective rate is 2.106. Your bill uses the general rate times the assessed value, not the price.

The effective rate is the one to compare towns with. Then ask for the home's actual tax bill before you offer.

Talk to a licensed lender for your numbers.
